malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dynamic code execution via eval, especially with decoded or obfuscated payloads, is a common technique for hiding malicious actions and evading static analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should avoid using eval, particularly with dynamically decoded or untrusted content, due to the high risk of arbitrary code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some template engines or interpreters may use eval, but only with strict input validation and clear documentation.

package_info.why_malicious: This report does not analyze a specific malicious package, but instead details GuardDog's detection heuristics for identifying malicious behaviors in npm and PyPI packages. The heuristics focus on behaviors such as exfiltration of environment variables, silent execution of binaries, dynamic code execution, and unauthorized install scripts, all of which are commonly observed in malicious packages.

Compare published package contents with the public source repository to detect unauthorized modifications or unexplained files. Monitor network activity for suspicious outbound requests to hardcoded or non-standard domains during installation or runtime.

package_info.why_malicious: The campaign leverages stolen GitHub personal access tokens to inject malicious GitHub Actions workflows and append obfuscated JavaScript code to hundreds of repositories. The injected workflow exfiltrates all repository secrets and variables to an attacker-controlled server on every push event, while the patched JavaScript files load a remote payload that intercepts user credentials from password forms and exfiltrates them. The attacker disguises these commits as Dependabot updates to evade detection, resulting in a large-scale supply chain attack targeting both CI/CD secrets and end-user credentials.

attack_chain.action: Attacker obtains developer's GitHub personal access token (likely via a malicious package or environment compromise).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can authenticate as the victim on GitHub.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses stolen token to push fake Dependabot commits to victim's repositories, adding a malicious GitHub Actions workflow and appending obfuscated code to JavaScript files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is present in the repository and will execute on CI/CD and in browsers.

attack_chain.action: On every push, the malicious GitHub Action exfiltrates repository secrets and variables to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive repository secrets.

attack_chain.action: When end-users load the compromised JavaScript files in their browsers, the appended code loads a remote script that intercepts password forms and exfiltrates credentials.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives user credentials submitted via web forms.

behavioral_signatures: Creation or modification of GitHub Actions workflow files that POST secrets or variables to external, non-corporate domains
Mass modification of *.js files with appended obfuscated code that injects a script tag loading a remote payload
Commits with fake Dependabot or bot-like messages introducing suspicious workflow or JavaScript changes
Browser JavaScript code that hooks password forms and sends serialized credentials to unknown endpoints
file_indicators: Any *.js file with appended obfuscated code that injects a script tag referencing send.wagateway.pro/client.js
Script tags in HTML referencing send.wagateway.pro/client.js
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for new or modified GitHub Actions workflows that POST secrets or variables to external domains. Scan repository JavaScript files for appended obfuscated code that injects remote scripts, especially those referencing send.wagateway.pro. Flag commits with bot-like or fake Dependabot messages that introduce such changes. In browser environments, detect scripts that hook password forms and send data to non-corporate endpoints. Block or alert on network traffic to known malicious domains such as send.wagateway.pro. Correlate these indicators to identify supply chain compromise.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines obfuscated helper functions to dynamically access Node.js filesystem methods (readdirSync, existsSync, readFileSync), enabling stealthy file system access and evasion of static analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscating method names for standard library functions is a common tactic to evade static analysis and hide malicious intent, making it harder for defenders to detect file system access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not obfuscate access to core Node.js modules or dynamically construct method names for standard APIs.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary code to protect intellectual property, but not in open-source utility libraries where transparency is expected.
key_indicators: Dynamic construction of method names for fs module
Helper functions that mask real API calls

package_info.package_versions: all published versions (as of report time)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of the legitimate 'chalk' package, published by an impersonated author account. It contains obfuscated code in 'index.esm.js' that, at import-time, initializes a Sentry SDK with a hardcoded DSN, accesses the user's filesystem, reads potentially sensitive files, intercepts console output, and exfiltrates this data to an external Sentry instance without user consent. The package copies the README and structure of the real 'chalk' package to deceive users and compromise their data.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious 'chalk-node' package, triggering execution of index.esm.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sentry is initialized with a hardcoded DSN and obfuscated file system access helpers are set up, preparing the environment for data exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Whenever console.log is called, the overridden function reads files from a '../data' directory and checks log arguments for sensitive patterns.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive file contents and log data are prepared for exfiltration to the attacker's Sentry instance.

attack_chain.action: File contents and/or log data are sent to the attacker's Sentry instance, using chunked messages and obfuscated prefixes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives exfiltrated data; user remains unaware due to silent error handling and obfuscated code.

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated access to Node.js fs module methods (readdirSync, existsSync, readFileSync) via dynamically constructed function names
Overriding of console.log with hidden file system access and network exfiltration side effects
File system reads from '../data' directory triggered by logging activity
Network requests to Sentry or other telemetry endpoints with hardcoded DSNs at import-time
Silent error handling (empty catch blocks) in code paths handling sensitive data or network operations
Freezing of the console object to prevent further modification
file_indicators: Presence of index.esm.js with obfuscated and minified code
Unexpected initialization of @sentry/node in utility packages
References to '../data' directory access in code
Obfuscated helper functions for fs module access
network_indicators: Outbound requests to o4505703178960896.ingest.sentry.io or similar Sentry DSNs
Unusual volume of Sentry.captureMessage calls from utility packages
Data exfiltration patterns using chunked messages and obfuscated prefixes in Sentry events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that override console.log or other standard output functions, especially if they access the filesystem or send data to external telemetry services. Flag any use of obfuscated or dynamically constructed method names for core modules (e.g., fs['readFileSync']). Alert on unexpected initialization of @sentry/node or similar telemetry SDKs in utility libraries. Watch for outbound network requests to hardcoded Sentry DSNs or other suspicious endpoints, particularly if accompanied by chunked or obfuscated payloads. Use static analysis to detect empty catch blocks in code that handles sensitive data or network operations. Scan for references to '../data' directory access and freezing of the console object in package code.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Greatness (N/A (Phishing-as-a-Service toolkit, not a traditional package manager))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the script decodes Base64-encoded strings to reconstruct code, then dynamically loads additional obfuscated JavaScript libraries from attacker-controlled servers, complicating both static and dynamic analysis and enabling modular delivery of malicious logic.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscation and dynamic loading from non-standard domains are classic evasion techniques, making it difficult for analysts and automated tools to inspect or block the malicious logic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate sites may use code splitting or load libraries from trusted CDNs, but do not obfuscate core authentication logic or load critical scripts from untrusted, attacker-controlled domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate applications use dynamic loading for performance, but not for sensitive authentication flows or from untrusted sources.
key_indicators: Dynamic script loading from unfamiliar or non-standard domains
Obfuscated logic in core authentication or credential handling code

package_info.package_manager: N/A (Phishing-as-a-Service toolkit, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: Greatness is a Phishing-as-a-Service toolkit explicitly designed to facilitate credential theft by mimicking Microsoft 365 login pages, intercepting multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes, and employing advanced evasion techniques such as JavaScript obfuscation, anti-bot logic, dynamic content loading, and encrypted exfiltration. Its sole purpose is to enable unauthorized access to Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing user credentials and session data.

attack_chain.action: Victim receives a phishing email or PDF containing a QR code that directs them to a malicious login page designed to mimic Microsoft 365.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim visits the phishing site.

attack_chain.action: Phishing site loads obfuscated and dynamically loaded JavaScript, implements anti-bot and CAPTCHA evasion to avoid automated detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim is presented with a fake Microsoft 365 login page.

attack_chain.action: Victim enters credentials and MFA code into the fake login form, which captures and prepares the data for exfiltration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials and MFA code are captured by the phishing kit.

attack_chain.action: Captured credentials and MFA code are encrypted, packaged with a JWT, and exfiltrated to the attacker's server using AJAX POST requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives credentials and session data.

attack_chain.action: Attacker is notified via Telegram bot of new stolen credentials, enabling rapid exploitation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker uses credentials and session cookie to access the victim's Microsoft 365 account.

behavioral_signatures: Phishing pages that closely mimic Microsoft 365 login, capturing both credentials and MFA codes
Obfuscated JavaScript with dynamic loading of additional code from non-standard or attacker-controlled domains
Use of CAPTCHA and custom anti-bot logic to evade automated security analysis and sandboxes
AJAX POST requests containing encrypted payloads (e.g., AES-encrypted JSON) sent to unknown or non-Microsoft endpoints after credential input
Outbound HTTP requests to the Telegram Bot API (api.telegram.org) containing credential data for attacker notification
file_indicators: HTML attachments or web pages with Microsoft 365 branding but source code or form actions pointing to non-Microsoft domains
PDF documents containing QR codes that resolve to suspicious or non-Microsoft URLs
JavaScript files or inline scripts with heavy obfuscation, Base64-encoded strings, or dynamic script loading from unfamiliar domains
network_indicators: AJAX or fetch requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., attacker.com, cdn.attacker.com) not associated with Microsoft
Outbound connections to api.telegram.org with embedded bot tokens and chat IDs
Dynamic script loading from domains not associated with trusted CDNs or Microsoft infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for phishing emails or PDF attachments containing QR codes that direct users to non-Microsoft login pages. Analyze web traffic for AJAX POST requests with encrypted payloads (such as AES-encrypted JSON) to unknown or suspicious domains, especially following credential or MFA input. Flag any use of the Telegram Bot API for outbound notifications from web pages, particularly when containing credential data. Detect obfuscated JavaScript and dynamic script loading from non-standard or attacker-controlled sources. Employ sandboxing and behavioral analysis to identify anti-bot and CAPTCHA evasion logic, and correlate with file and network indicators for comprehensive detection.
